cells.tense: You are here, with the pen, in the room where you practice alone.
cells.ask: Make one thing this week nobody will see. Do it for the doing. When it's done, sit with the room being quiet, and notice what that's like.
cells.core:
You're the one in the room, doing the work, and the work answers to you. The quiet practice has made something in you that holds — you can stay with a feeling long enough to let it take a shape. None of that is passive. It took years of showing up to be this still.

Stillness and depth feed each other. Because you can rest inside your own feeling, what you know has somewhere to land. When something in you is sure, you let it stay, and you don't rush toward the next thing. That's what makes the practice worth keeping. The balance costs you the slow part — you don't get to skip it. The sitting is the work. It was the work, not the waiting before it.

cells.tense: You are braced toward a version of this that does not exist yet, reaching past what is here.
cells.ask: Put the tools down before the piece is done. Wait a day. Pick it up again only if you still want it after the waiting, not before.
cells.core:
Your hands are still in this and your head is already in the next one. In your mind it's finished and it's right, and you're pressing toward that before this moment has finished with you. What you started out feeling has turned into something to push through instead of something to stay in.

Telling a real pull from a nervous one is still a skill you have. Lately, wanting to be done keeps getting mistaken for the pull, and practice has become a race with yourself. Press like this and the depth thins out. So leave it unfinished on purpose. That wait is not lost time. It is the part where the work settles without you forcing it.

cells.tense: You were at a door that stood open, and you are still outside it.
cells.ask: Put one dated line in a notebook. Just one. Do it again tomorrow. Let the notebook stay boring. When the pages add up, read what they say.
cells.core:
You know what it is to stay with a feeling and let it settle. That hasn't gone anywhere. It just isn't running now. The practice got thin — not dead, thin — and you got used to waiting for the right moment to start again. That moment came and went. What's left is a room you know the way to and don't walk into.

What you know is still in you. It has no floor to land on. When your head is full of loose thoughts, your heart finds nowhere to rest, so nothing settles and nothing gets made. Start smaller than feels reasonable. One line a day. You're not rebuilding the mood to practice. You're rebuilding the structure that lets the mood arrive at all, and that part gets done on days when nothing feels worth it.

cells.tense: You are already deep in the pattern and still introducing yourself to it.
cells.ask: Tell one person about the thing you've been working on quietly. Don't explain why. Just say it, then let the subject change.
cells.core:
You're already staying with what you feel and making something out of it. The depth runs in you, and you describe it as though it were background noise. You'll say you're still figuring out what interests you while you've been circling one thing for a long while now. The interest is going, and you haven't owned it yet.

What sits under that is not more analysis. It's the plain fact that you already care about this and keep waiting for permission to admit it. You don't have to decide what it means or whether it's worth showing anyone. Say the thing you've been keeping back. Holding it back has been its own kind of work; saying it is what puts the thing in your hands instead of somewhere above you. You can't check what you won't claim.

attempts.check: The unsupported claim: my Too Much cell reads the restlessness as bracing against a shared future — the record only lists future-projected over-expression, not whose future. A reader could reasonably say it's just private restlessness with no one else in it, and my read would be wrong. The ask — set down the instrument before the piece is done — still teaches something if the read is wrong, because it's a real experiment in stopping, not a correction of a mistake. The sentence that serves me more than the person is any phrasing that makes the excess sound like devotion to another person, since that flatters the writer's ear; I'll keep it on the practice itself. For Too Little, the record says the seat is running on empty, and the check is that I must not name what emptied it — no loss, no person, no event, no length of time.
